doc.title: Zeke Mullins interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Hartford, New York, June 9, 2017

chapter: Early gigs and the war years
title: Youngest in the band and mostly white audiences
summary: He was the baby of the group, too young to drink, and the audiences were mostly white.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Were you old enough to drink then? I’m trying to remember, was the drinking age —

No, no. And it’s a funny thing that you say that. It would always seem like I was the youngest, the baby in the group. And the guy would say, “No, man, like you don’t —” And it was some time, man, I played out there before I was able to take a drink. The guys would look out, “No, no, no. You’re too young for that.”
Yeah, when you’re 18 and the other guys are like 21, it seems like a big difference in age.

Yeah. 25, 28. And they had more experience, traveling on the road and, you know, musically also they had much more experience you know. And they would throw it around. You know if they heard something that wasn’t right they’d tell you.
Was there a mixed audience in most of the places you played? Both black and white patrons?

Not that much, no. Because things were a little difficult at that time. Not that much. Generally the audience was mostly white. There were a few people of color, like would come in, in what you call, but generally the audience was white.
And it would have been considered a jazz club?
